doc.title: J. Leo Rayhill interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 23, 2007

title: Dorm life, campus news and Hal Wagner's convertible
summary: A Victrola was his top dorm gadget; roommate Hal Wagner, a Battle of the Bulge veteran, owned a convertible.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: You know the look of a dorm room has changed an awful lot. I think about my daughter went here, and I think about what we moved up to campus for her, included a refrigerator and I mean a computer, the whole thing. I’m just curious, what was the most high tech thing you would have had in your dorm room at that time?
It had a lampshade I think, which covered the lamp that we read by and also —
Oh you would wear it on occasion, when Gene Romano came by. Did you have telephones in the room?
No. We had the telephones down the hall, and always there was a line waiting.

It’s so interesting to think back then. Like you know a couple of weeks ago Hamilton had a very rare day when they closed the campus down. And they canceled classes ‘cause of the weather. And of course that kind of news these days just spreads so quickly, you © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
know, everybody’s got email and all that, and I just wondered like how did news spread around the campus? Just word of mouth?
Yeah, yeah. That’s about it, it’s word of mouth.
Yeah. Like if a class was canceled you’d probably just find out when you went there.
Okay. Did you own a car at the time?

No I did not. No. I never owned a car until later, much later, after I got out of school. But Hal Wagner, and Frank Fry, and my wonderful roommate, had a convertible and we were the toast of the campus for that I’ll tell you. How he ever sprung for it, but he was a great guy. He was a veteran. He’d come back. He’d served in the Battle of the Bulge and he had — both his legs had been severely damaged from the war, but he was a great guy and he was fun. He looked like Fred Astaire, and my fondest memory of him was dancing on the Psi U house’s roof at a house party. He was just — he was a very good dancer, a very handsome guy, and everybody loved him. You meet very few of them in your lifetime. He was just a delightful guy.
How do you spell his last name?
